html:
The big picture

A function f : X \to Y assigns exactly one output to each input, and it is not just a formula: it is a formula together with a domain (allowed inputs) and a codomain (target set). The range is the set of outputs that are actually reached, and the graph \Gamma(f) is the set of all input–output pairs; the vertical line test tells which curves are graphs. Curves that are not graphs, such as the circle, can still be described by parametric equations. Three properties then depend on the chosen domain and codomain: injective (no output is hit twice), surjective (every target is hit) and bijective (both); the horizontal line test checks them on a graph. Further properties describe shape: increasing/decreasing, even/odd, bounded. The lecture surveys the common families (affine, power, polynomial, rational, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic, hyperbolic) and then builds new functions from old ones: operations f+g, fg, f/g (where the domain is the puzzle), graph transformations (shifts, stretches, reflections, sine waves), composition f \circ g and the inverse function f^{-1}, which exists exactly for bijections and often needs a restricted domain (the arc functions). It closes with elementary vs. non-elementary functions.

Why functions?

A function connects a quantity we control or observe to an output.

Everyday / engineering examples:

  • time \mapsto temperature;
  • time \mapsto position of a robot;
  • input voltage \mapsto output voltage;
  • side length \mapsto area.

A mathematical model: A(s) = s^2, s \ge 0; A(2) = 4, A(3) = 9.

A function is not just a formula: it is an assignment.

Where engineers meet functions

A chosen input is mapped to an output by a mathematical rule.

Neural networksMotionAC voltage
Input x \mapsto activation aTime t \mapsto position sTime t \mapsto voltage u
a(x) = \max\{0, x\}s(t) = 2t^2u(t) = 10 \sin(2\pi t)
ReLU: negative inputs become zeroConstant acceleration from restPeriodic electrical signal

The same function idea appears in AI, motion and electrical signals.

What is a function?

A function f : X \to Y assigns exactly one element f(x) \in Y to each x \in X.

Board. Definition: a function f : X \to Y is a rule that assigns exactly one element of Y to each element of X. Example: X = \{1, 2, 3\}, Y = \{1, 4, 9\}, f : X \to Y, f(x) = x^2: 1 \mapsto 1, 2 \mapsto 4, 3 \mapsto 9. Notation: f : X \to Y, x \mapsto f(x), y = f(x). One input cannot have two different outputs.

Two different inputs may have the same output. But one input cannot have two outputs.

Intuition — two conditions hidden in "exactly one"

"Exactly one output for each input" is two demands: each x \in X gets an output (none is left out), and it gets only one (no input has two). As a set, f is a subset of the product X \times Y (2 Elements of Sets) that contains, for every x \in X, exactly one pair (x, y). Nothing is said about the y's: some may be hit several times, some never.

Common mistake — "a function is its formula"

Tempting: f(x) = x^2 is the function. But "x^2" says nothing about which x are allowed or where the values may land, and both change the answers to every later question (range, injective, inverse). The function is the triple (domain, codomain, rule). The slides make the point with three functions that share the formula x^2 but differ in domain (below).

Domain, codomain, range

For f : X \to Y:

  • X = domain;
  • Y = codomain;
  • f(X) = range (actual outputs): f(X) = \{f(x) : x \in X\} \subseteq Y.

Example: f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, f(x) = x^2: \operatorname{dom}(f) = \mathbb{R}, \operatorname{ran}(f) = [0, \infty), codomain = \mathbb{R}. The codomain can be larger than the range.

Domain = allowed inputs; range = attained outputs.

Board. X = D(f) = \operatorname{dom}(f) – domain: allowed inputs. Y – codomain: specified target set. R(f) = \operatorname{ran}(f) = f(X) – range: actual outputs, R(f) = \{f(x) : x \in D(f)\} \subseteq Y. Example: f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, f(x) = x^2; D(f) = \mathbb{R}, codomain = \mathbb{R}, R(f) = [0, \infty). Range \subseteq codomain; they need not be equal.

Common mistake — range and codomain are not the same

The codomain is declared ("the values lie somewhere in \mathbb{R}"); the range is computed (which values actually occur). For f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, f(x) = x^2, the codomain is \mathbb{R}, but -1 is never reached, so the range is only [0, \infty). "Find the range" therefore always means work: solve f(x) = y and ask for which y it has a solution.

Same formula, different function

The rule f(x) = x^2 does not determine the function without a domain and codomain.

FunctionRange
f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, f(x) = x^2[0, \infty)
g : [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty), g(x) = x^2[0, \infty)
h : \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\} \to \mathbb{R}, h(x) = x^2\{0, 1, 4\}

All use the same formula!

Board. The same three functions drawn: the full parabola for f, only the right half for g, and five separate dots for h, with D(h) = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}, R(h) = \{0, 1, 4\}.

Domain practice

Find the natural real domain of each formula.

FormulaDomain
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}
g(x) = \sqrt{4 - x}(-\infty, 4]
h(x) = \sqrt{1 - x^2}[-1, 1]
p(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}(2, \infty)

For roots: radicand \ge 0. For denominators: never zero.

Intuition — natural domain

When only a formula is given, its natural (maximal) domain is the set of all real x for which the formula can be evaluated. Collect every restriction as an inequality and intersect them: an even root needs radicand \ge 0, a denominator must be \neq 0, and (later in this lecture) a logarithm needs a positive argument.

Worked example — natural domain of f(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x+3}}{x-1}
  1. List the restrictions: the root needs x + 3 \ge 0; the denominator needs x - 1 \neq 0.
  2. Solve each: x \ge -3; x \neq 1.
  3. Intersect: [-3, \infty) \setminus \{1\} = [-3, 1) \cup (1, \infty). Note that p(x) in the table has the root in the denominator, so there the two conditions combine to the strict x - 2 > 0.

What does the range look like?

For each graph, look at all the y-values that are actually reached.

Worked example — reading off the four ranges

Project the graph onto the y-axis: which heights does the curve reach?

  1. x^2: every height \ge 0, and 0 itself at x = 0 → [0, \infty).
  2. 1/x: every height except 0 (1/x = y gives x = 1/y, which needs y \neq 0) → \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}.
  3. \sqrt{x} on x \ge 0: 0 at x = 0, then all positive heights (\sqrt{x} = y gives x = y^2 for every y \ge 0) → [0, \infty). The plot stops at x = 4, the function doesn't.
  4. \sqrt{4 - x^2} on \lvert x\rvert \le 2: highest point 2 at x = 0, lowest 0 at x = \pm 2, and everything in between → [0, 2].

The graph of a function

\Gamma(f) = \{(x, f(x)) : x \in \operatorname{dom}(f)\}.
Symbols
  • \Gamma(f) — the graph of f (Greek capital gamma): a set of points in the plane
  • (x, f(x)) — the ordered pair "input, output"; one point of the graph
  • \operatorname{dom}(f) — the domain of f; x runs through all of it

The graph consists of input–output pairs. For f(x) = x^2: (-2, 4), (-1, 1), (0, 0), (1, 1).

Board. For f : X \to Y, the graph is \Gamma(f) = \{(x, f(x)) : x \in D(f)\} \subseteq X \times Y.

Vertical line test

A curve is the graph of a function of x exactly when every vertical line meets it at most once.

Board. Vertical line test: a curve is the graph of a function y = f(x) if and only if every vertical line intersects it at most once. The board shows three cases: a circle (not a function), y = x^2 and y = \sqrt{x} (functions). Not every curve is a graph: a sideways parabola has two y-values for some x.

Why does the vertical line test work?

A vertical line x = a collects exactly the points of the curve with input a. Two intersection points (a, y_1) and (a, y_2) with y_1 \neq y_2 would mean one input with two outputs, which a function forbids. Zero intersections are allowed: that just means a is not in the domain. So "at most once" is exactly the condition "no input has two outputs".

Beyond graphs of functions

Consider the circle x^2 + y^2 = 1. It is a curve in the plane. Question: is the full circle the graph of one function y = f(x)?

No. When x = \frac12, the circle has two values: y = \pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.

A curve need not be the graph of a function y = f(x).

Intuition — cut the circle in half

Solving x^2 + y^2 = 1 for y gives two answers, y = \sqrt{1 - x^2} and y = -\sqrt{1 - x^2}. Each half separately is a function on [-1, 1] (upper and lower semicircle); only the whole circle fails. The fourth range graph above, \sqrt{4 - x^2}, is exactly such an upper half (of the circle with radius 2).

Parametric equations

We describe a point using one parameter t: \bigl(x(t), y(t)\bigr).

Example: the unit circle. x(t) = \cos t, y(t) = \sin t, 0 \le t < 2\pi.

Why a circle? x(t)^2 + y(t)^2 = \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1.

What changes with t? The point travels counterclockwise.

A moving object: position depends on time

A simple horizontal launch: x(t) = 3t, y(t) = 4 - 5t^2, 0 \le t \le \sqrt{4/5} (seconds). At time t the position is (x(t), y(t)).

Eliminating t: t = x/3, y = 4 - \frac{5}{9}x^2.

The equations describe where the object is and how it moves as time passes.

Board. Cycloid (point on a rolling wheel): x(t) = R(t - \sin t), y(t) = R(1 - \cos t). A cycloid consists of repeated arches.

Intuition — what a parametrisation adds

A graph y = f(x) only says which points lie on the curve. A parametrisation also says when and in which direction each point is visited, like a recording of a robot's path with time stamps. That is why the circle needs no splitting here: the parameter t is an input with exactly one output point (\cos t, \sin t), even though some x-values occur twice.

Why does the launch end at t = \sqrt{4/5}?

The object hits the ground when y(t) = 0: 4 - 5t^2 = 0 gives t^2 = 4/5, so t = \sqrt{4/5} \approx 0.894 s (the negative root is before the launch). At that moment x = 3\sqrt{4/5} \approx 2.68 m, the landing point on the plot.

Worked example — eliminating the parameter

x(t) = 1 + 2t, y(t) = t^2.

  1. Solve the simpler equation for t: t = \dfrac{x - 1}{2}.
  2. Substitute into the other: y = \left(\dfrac{x - 1}{2}\right)^2.
  3. Read the curve: a parabola with vertex at (1, 0), traced from left to right as t increases.

One circle, three descriptions

DescriptionEquation
Cartesianx^2 + y^2 = 1
Parametricx(t) = \cos t, y(t) = \sin t
Polarr = 1, 0 \le \theta < 2\pi

In polar coordinates, x = r\cos\theta and y = r\sin\theta.

Different descriptions, same geometric curve.

Connection

The polar description is the same (r, \theta) as the polar form of a complex number in 4 Complex Numbers: the unit circle is the set of all e^{i\theta}.

Piecewise-defined functions

f(x) = \begin{cases} -x, & x < 0, \\ x^2, & 0 \le x \le 1, \\ 1, & x > 1. \end{cases}
Symbols
  • x — the input (a real number); which line applies depends on where x lies
  • f(x) — the output; each input uses exactly one of the three formulas

\operatorname{dom}(f) = \mathbb{R}, \operatorname{ran}(f) = [0, \infty).

One function can use several formulas on different inputs.

Common mistake — overlapping or missing cases

The conditions of a piecewise definition must split the domain cleanly: every x in exactly one case. Here x < 0, 0 \le x \le 1, x > 1 do that; 0 and 1 belong to the middle line. If two cases overlapped and gave different values (say x \le 1 and x \ge 1 with different formulas at 1), the "function" would have two outputs at 1 and wouldn't be a function.

Floor and ceiling: small changes, big jumps

Floor \lfloor x \rfloor: greatest integer \le x. \lfloor 2.7 \rfloor = 2, \lfloor -1.2 \rfloor = -2.

Ceiling \lceil x \rceil: least integer \ge x. \lceil 2.7 \rceil = 3, \lceil -1.2 \rceil = -1.

Common mistake — floor is not "drop the decimals"

For positive numbers floor and cutting off agree (\lfloor 2.7 \rfloor = 2). For negative numbers they don't: \lfloor -3.5 \rfloor = -4, because -4 is the greatest integer below -3.5; cutting off would give -3. Picture the number line: floor always moves left to the next integer, ceiling always right (unless x is already an integer).

Injective, surjective, bijective

Injective (one-to-one): f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2. — Injective: no repeated output from different inputs.

Surjective (onto): \forall y \in Y\ \exists x \in X : f(x) = y. — Surjective: every target is hit.

Bijective: both injective and surjective.

All three notions depend on the stated domain and codomain.

Board. Injective (one-to-one): for f : X \to Y, x_1 \neq x_2 \Rightarrow f(x_1) \neq f(x_2). Equivalently, f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2. Example: f(x) = 2x + 1 is injective on \mathbb{R}. Counterexample: g(x) = x^2 on \mathbb{R} is not injective since g(-1) = g(1).

Why are the two injectivity conditions the same?

"x_1 \neq x_2 \Rightarrow f(x_1) \neq f(x_2)" and "f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2" are contrapositives of each other (A \Rightarrow B is equivalent to \neg B \Rightarrow \neg A, 1 Elements of Logic). The second form is the one used in proofs, because it starts from an equation you can calculate with.

Worked example — f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, f(x) = 5 - 3x is bijective
  1. Injective — start from equal outputs: 5 - 3x_1 = 5 - 3x_2 \Rightarrow -3x_1 = -3x_2 \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2.
  2. Surjective — take any target y and solve f(x) = y: 5 - 3x = y \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{5 - y}{3}, which is a real number for every y \in \mathbb{R}.
  3. Check it really hits y: f\!\left(\dfrac{5 - y}{3}\right) = 5 - (5 - y) = y. ✓
  4. Conclude: injective and surjective, so bijective. (To disprove injectivity, one pair x_1 \neq x_2 with equal outputs is enough, like g(-1) = g(1) on the board.)

A quick check

Mapping X = \{1, 2, 3\} \to Y = \{a, b, c\} with 1 \mapsto a, 2 \mapsto a, 3 \mapsto c. Question: is this mapping injective? Surjective? Bijective?

Not injective (1 and 2 map to a). Not surjective (b is never reached).

The horizontal line test

At most one intersection \Rightarrow injective; every height in the codomain reached \Rightarrow surjective.

Board. Let f : X \to Y be a real-valued function. Consider horizontal lines y = c with c \in Y.

  • At most one intersection with every such line \Rightarrow injective.
  • At least one intersection with every such line \Rightarrow surjective onto Y.
  • Exactly one intersection with every such line \Rightarrow bijective.

Examples: x^2 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} — neither; x^2 : \mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty) — onto, not one-to-one; e^x : \mathbb{R} \to (0, \infty) — bijective.

Intuition — vertical vs. horizontal

The vertical test asks about inputs (is f a function at all?); the horizontal test asks about outputs (how often is each value hit?). A horizontal line y = c meets the graph exactly at the solutions of f(x) = c. So "how many intersections" is "how many solutions", and injective/surjective/bijective mean "at most one / at least one / exactly one solution for every c in the codomain". Only lines at heights c in the codomain count, which is why changing the codomain changes surjectivity.

The same formula can become bijective

Functioninjectivesurjective
f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, f(x) = x^2××
f : \mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty), f(x) = x^2×✓
g : [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty), g(x) = x^2✓✓

Restricting the domain and choosing the right codomain can turn a function into a bijection.

Connection

Shrinking the codomain to the range always makes a function surjective; shrinking the domain to a part where the function is strictly monotone (next section) makes it injective. This is exactly the recipe for the inverse functions at the end of the lecture (\sqrt{x}, \arcsin, \arccos, \arctan).

Increasing and decreasing functions

Let I \subseteq D(f) be an interval. For every x_1, x_2 \in I with x_1 < x_2:

non-strictstrict
increasingNon-decreasing (weakly increasing): f(x_1) \le f(x_2)Strictly increasing: f(x_1) < f(x_2)
decreasingNon-increasing (weakly decreasing): f(x_1) \ge f(x_2)Strictly decreasing: f(x_1) > f(x_2)

Examples: x^2 is strictly decreasing on (-\infty, 0] and strictly increasing on [0, \infty). A constant function satisfies both non-strict definitions.

Why is a strictly monotone function injective?

If x_1 \neq x_2, one of them is smaller, say x_1 < x_2. Strictly increasing gives f(x_1) < f(x_2), strictly decreasing gives f(x_1) > f(x_2); either way f(x_1) \neq f(x_2). That is the board's form of injectivity. (A non-decreasing function needn't be injective: a constant function isn't.)

Common mistake — monotone on two pieces, monotone everywhere?

f(x) = 1/x is strictly decreasing on (-\infty, 0) and on (0, \infty). Tempting conclusion: it is decreasing on its whole domain. It isn't: -1 < 1 but f(-1) = -1 < 1 = f(1). The definition compares any two points of one set, including one from each piece; that is why the slide asks for an interval I.

Applications: how quantities change

Three simple models. What happens to each output as time increases?

Distance travelledFuel remainingParking charge
s(t) = 2tF(t) = 10 - 2tP(t) = 2\lceil t \rceil
t in seconds; s in metrest in hours; F in litrest in hours; P in euros
Strictly increasingStrictly decreasingNon-decreasing

A non-decreasing function may be constant on an interval and may also have jumps.

Intuition — the parking charge

P(t) = 2\lceil t \rceil: every started hour costs 2 €. Parking 1.5 h and 2 h both cost 4 €, so P is flat on each hour (not strictly increasing) and jumps to 6 € just after 2 h. It never goes down, which is all "non-decreasing" asks.

Even and odd functions: symmetry

For f, g : D \to \mathbb{R}, assume x \in D implies -x \in D.

  • Even: symmetry about the y-axis: f(-x) = f(x) for all x \in D. Example: f(x) = x^2, with f(-1) = f(1) = 1.
  • Odd: symmetry about the origin: g(-x) = -g(x) for all x \in D. Example: g(x) = x^3, with g(-1) = -g(1).

A function may be even, odd, or neither.

Intuition — why the domain must be symmetric

Both definitions compare the values at x and -x, so -x must be allowed whenever x is. \sqrt{x} on [0, \infty) is therefore neither even nor odd, before any calculation.

Worked example — testing symmetry

Method: compute f(-x), simplify, compare with f(x) and with -f(x).

  1. f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 1} (domain \mathbb{R}, symmetric): f(-x) = \dfrac{-x}{x^2 + 1} = -f(x) → odd.
  2. h(x) = x^3 + x^2: h(-x) = -x^3 + x^2. That equals neither h(x) = x^3 + x^2 nor -h(x) = -x^3 - x^2 (test at x = 1: h(-1) = 0, h(1) = 2) → neither. A sum of an odd and an even part with both present is neither; one counterexample x is enough to show it.

Bounded and unbounded functions

A function f : D \to \mathbb{R} is

  • bounded from above: \exists M \in \mathbb{R}\ \forall x \in D : f(x) \le M;
  • bounded from below: \exists m \in \mathbb{R}\ \forall x \in D : f(x) \ge m;
  • bounded: \exists M \in \mathbb{R}\ \forall x \in D : \lvert f(x)\rvert \le M;
  • unbounded means not bounded.
Example
f(x) = \sin x: -1 \le f(x) \le 1bounded above and below
f(x) = x^2: f(x) \ge 0bounded below, not above
f(x) = -x^2: f(x) \le 0bounded above, not below
f(x) = x: no upper or lower boundneither bound (unbounded both ways)
Connection

These are the bounds of 3 Set of Real Numbers applied to the range: f is bounded above exactly when the set f(D) is bounded above. So \sup f(D) exists by completeness. Example: \frac{1}{1 + x^2} on \mathbb{R} has range (0, 1]: bounded, with maximum 1 and infimum 0 (never attained).

Why is "bounded" the same as "bounded above and below"?

If \lvert f(x)\rvert \le M, then -M \le f(x) \le M: both bounds. Conversely, if m \le f(x) \le M' for all x, take M = \max\{\lvert m\rvert, \lvert M'\rvert\}; then -M \le m \le f(x) \le M' \le M, i.e. \lvert f(x)\rvert \le M. The order of the quantifiers matters: one M must work for all x ("\exists M\ \forall x"). For f(x) = x every single x has some bound above it, but no single bound works for all.

Common families of functions

Affine functions

A function f(x) = mx + b, with constants m, b \in \mathbb{R}, is called a linear (affine) function.

Graphs: different slopes y = mx for m = -1, 1/2, 1, 2; special cases y = x and y = 1.5 (identity and constant function).

f(x) = x is the identity; f(x) = b is constant; f(x) = mx describes proportionality (m > 0).

Power functions

A power function has the form f(x) = x^k (on its real domain).

Natural exponents k = n \in \mathbb{N}. For n \ge 1, D(f) = \mathbb{R}. Compare the symmetry of even and odd powers: for f(x) = x^n, an even n gives f(-x) = f(x); an odd n gives f(-x) = -f(x). Graphs: x^2 and x^4 (both even functions), x^3 and x^5 (both odd functions). Compare what happens near x = 0 and for \lvert x\rvert > 1.

Negative integer exponents satisfy x^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{x^n} for n \in \mathbb{N}, n \ge 1, provided x \neq 0.

Exponent -1Exponent -2
functiony = x^{-1} = 1/xy = x^{-2} = 1/x^2
domain, rangeD = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}; R = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}D = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}; R = (0, \infty)

Rational exponents k = \frac{p}{q} \in \mathbb{Q}: the real domain of x^k depends on the exponent. Roots can change the allowed inputs.

Square rootCube rootExponent 3/2Exponent 2/3
functiony = x^{1/2} = \sqrt{x}y = x^{1/3} = \sqrt[3]{x}y = x^{3/2}y = x^{2/3}
domain, rangeD = [0, \infty), R = [0, \infty)D = \mathbb{R}, R = \mathbb{R}D = [0, \infty), R = [0, \infty)D = \mathbb{R}, R = [0, \infty)

The denominator of a rational exponent matters for negative inputs.

Why does the denominator decide whether negative inputs are allowed?

x^{p/q} means \left(\sqrt[q]{x}\right)^p. For odd q, the q-th root of a negative number exists (\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2), so the whole real line is allowed; for even q it doesn't (no real y has y^2 = -4), so x \ge 0. The numerator only raises the result to a power, which is always possible. Hence x^{2/3} is defined on \mathbb{R} (and \ge 0, because of the even power 2), but x^{3/2} only on [0, \infty). (This assumes p/q in lowest terms.)

Polynomial functions

A polynomial is p(x) = a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1 x + a_0, where n \ge 0 is an integer and a_j \in \mathbb{R}.

Graphs: cubic x^3 - 3x (three real zeros); quartic x^4 - 2x^2 (even polynomial); (x + 1)^2(x - 1) (repeated root: touches at x = -1).

Every polynomial is defined for all real x; coefficients control its shape.

Intuition — what a repeated root looks like

At a simple zero the factor (x - a) changes sign, so the graph crosses the axis. At a double zero the factor (x - a)^2 is \ge 0 on both sides, so the graph only touches the axis and turns back, as (x + 1)^2(x - 1) does at x = -1. This is the real-axis picture of the multiplicities in 4 Complex Numbers.

Rational functions

A rational function has the form f(x) = \dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}, where p, q are polynomials. Values with q(x) = 0 are excluded.

Oblique asymptoteHorizontal asymptoteVertical asymptote
\dfrac{2x^2 - 3}{7x + 4} (orange: asymptote)\dfrac{5x^2 + 8x - 3}{3x^2 + 2} (orange: y = 5/3)\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 1} (x = 1 is excluded)

Asymptotes are shown in orange; not every rational function has every type.

Where do the asymptotes y = 5/3 and the oblique line come from?

For large \lvert x\rvert only the highest powers matter. Equal degrees: divide numerator and denominator by x^2: \dfrac{5 + 8/x - 3/x^2}{3 + 2/x^2} \to \dfrac{5}{3}, the ratio of the leading coefficients. Numerator degree one higher: polynomial division gives \dfrac{2x^2 - 3}{7x + 4} = \dfrac{2}{7}x - \dfrac{8}{49} - \dfrac{115/49}{7x + 4}; the last term goes to 0, so the graph approaches the line y = \frac27 x - \frac{8}{49}. Vertical: where the denominator is 0 and the numerator isn't (x = 1 for \frac{x+1}{x-1}), the values blow up. (Limits are made precise later; here this is the idea.)

Algebraic functions

An algebraic function is constructed from polynomials using finitely many algebraic operations and taking roots.

Graphs: product with a cube root, x^{1/3}(x - 4), defined for all x \in \mathbb{R}; fractional powers, \frac34 (x^2 - 1)^{2/3}, cusps at x = \pm 1.

Polynomials and rational functions are also algebraic functions.

Trigonometric functions

Trigonometric functions arise from the unit circle. They repeat their values periodically.

y = \cos xy = \sin xy = \tan x
domain\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}x \neq \pi/2 + k\pi
range[-1, 1][-1, 1]\mathbb{R}
period2\pi2\pi\pi

Angles are measured in radians. The tangent function is not defined at its vertical asymptotes.

More trigonometric functions. Secant, cosecant and cotangent are quotients of sine and cosine; their domains exclude zeros of the denominator.

\sec x = 1/\cos x\csc x = 1/\sin x\cot x = \cos x / \sin x
range(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\mathbb{R}

Fundamental periods: 2\pi for secant and cosecant, \pi for cotangent.

Why does \sec x never take values between -1 and 1?

\lvert\cos x\rvert \le 1, so \lvert\sec x\rvert = \dfrac{1}{\lvert\cos x\rvert} \ge 1 wherever it is defined. Dividing 1 by a number of size at most 1 gives something of size at least 1. The same argument works for \csc x with \sin x.

Exponential functions

An exponential function is f(x) = a^x, where a > 0 and a \neq 1. Every such function passes through (0, 1).

Graphs: growth a > 1: 2^x, 3^x, 10^x; decay 0 < a < 1: 2^{-x}, 3^{-x}, 10^{-x}.

D(f) = \mathbb{R}, R(f) = (0, \infty).

The natural exponential. The natural exponential function is e^x, with e \approx 2.71828. Models y = y_0 e^{kx} describe growth (k > 0) or decay (k < 0). Graphs: y = e^{0.75x} (outputs grow as x increases), y = e^{-0.75x} (outputs approach zero). y_0 > 0 is the initial value; these graphs use y_0 = 1.

Why does every exponential pass through (0, 1), and why are a = 1 and a \le 0 excluded?

a^0 = 1 for every a > 0, so the point (0, 1) is on every graph. a = 1 gives the constant function 1^x = 1, which is no "growth or decay" and not invertible. For a < 0, a^x is not real for many x ((-4)^{1/2}), and 0^x is 0 for x > 0 and undefined for x < 0. With a > 0, a \neq 1, the function is strictly monotone from \mathbb{R} onto (0, \infty), i.e. a bijection, which is what makes the logarithm (next) possible.

Logarithmic functions

A logarithmic function f(x) = \log_a x is the inverse of a^x for a > 0, a \neq 1. In particular, \ln x = \log_e x.

Graphs: increasing for a > 1: \log_2 x, \ln x, \log_{10} x; decreasing for 0 < a < 1: \log_{1/2} x, \log_{1/10} x.

D(f) = (0, \infty), R(f) = \mathbb{R}; all graphs pass through (1, 0).

Intuition — domain and range swap

Inverting a function swaps inputs and outputs. a^x takes all of \mathbb{R} to (0, \infty), so \log_a takes (0, \infty) to \mathbb{R}; and the point (0, 1) on the exponential becomes (1, 0) on the logarithm. That is why \log_a of a negative number or of 0 is undefined: no power of a is \le 0.

Hyperbolic functions

\cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}, \qquad \sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}.
Symbols
  • \cosh x — hyperbolic cosine of x (dimensionless; x real)
  • \sinh x — hyperbolic sine of x
  • e \approx 2.71828 — Euler's number, the base of the natural exponential

Graphs: \cosh x, even, minimum 1; \sinh x, odd, increasing.

Identity: \cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1. A hanging cable has the shape of a catenary.

Why is \cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1?

Expand both squares: \cosh^2 x = \frac{e^{2x} + 2 + e^{-2x}}{4} and \sinh^2 x = \frac{e^{2x} - 2 + e^{-2x}}{4} (using e^x e^{-x} = 1). Subtracting leaves \frac{2 - (-2)}{4} = 1. Compare \cos^2 x + \sin^2 x = 1: the point (\cosh t, \sinh t) moves on the hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1 the way (\cos t, \sin t) moves on the circle, hence the name. Evenness is visible in the formula too: swapping x \leftrightarrow -x swaps e^x and e^{-x}, which leaves the sum unchanged and flips the sign of the difference.

Useful identities: exponents and roots

Laws of exponents (a > 0):

  • a^s a^t = a^{s+t}
  • \dfrac{a^s}{a^t} = a^{s-t}
  • (a^s)^t = a^{st}
  • (ab)^s = a^s b^s (b > 0)

Roots (a, b \ge 0):

  • \sqrt[n]{a} = a^{1/n} (n \in \mathbb{N}, n \ge 1)
  • \sqrt{ab} = \sqrt{a}\sqrt{b}
  • \sqrt{a^2} = \lvert a\rvert (a \in \mathbb{R})
  • \sqrt{a + b} \neq \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} in general

Check the domain before applying a rule.

Common mistake — \sqrt{a^2} = a and \sqrt{a+b} = \sqrt a + \sqrt b

\sqrt{\;} always returns the non-negative root, so \sqrt{(-3)^2} = \sqrt9 = 3 = \lvert -3\rvert, not -3; that is why the slide writes \lvert a\rvert. And roots don't split over sums: \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5, but \sqrt9 + \sqrt{16} = 7. They do split over products (\sqrt{ab} = \sqrt a\sqrt b for a, b \ge 0), the same way powers split over products but not sums.

Useful identities: trigonometry

Basic identities:

  • \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1
  • \sin(-x) = -\sin x
  • \cos(-x) = \cos x
  • \tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} (\cos x \neq 0)
  • \sin(x + 2\pi) = \sin x

Angle addition:

  • \cos(u + v) = \cos u \cos v - \sin u \sin v
  • \sin(u + v) = \sin u \cos v + \cos u \sin v

Two useful special cases:

  • \sin(2x) = 2 \sin x \cos x
  • \cos(2x) = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x

Angles are in radians unless stated otherwise.

Connection

The special cases are the addition formulas with u = v = x. And \sin(-x) = -\sin x, \cos(-x) = \cos x say that sine is odd and cosine is even in the sense of the symmetry section. The addition formulas are also what makes "multiply complex numbers → add the angles" work in 4 Complex Numbers.

Operations with functions

On \operatorname{dom}(f) \cap \operatorname{dom}(g):

  • (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)
  • (f - g)(x) = f(x) - g(x)
  • (fg)(x) = f(x)g(x)
  • (cf)(x) = c\,f(x)
  • \left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} — for division: additionally g(x) \neq 0.

Always check the domain of the resulting function.

Operations: the domain is the puzzle

Let f(x) = \sqrt{x}, g(x) = \sqrt{1 - x}.

FunctionDomain
f + g, f - g, fg[0, 1]
\dfrac{f}{g}[0, 1)
\dfrac{g}{f}(0, 1]

The operation may exclude more inputs than either formula alone.

Why do the three domains differ?

\operatorname{dom}(f) = [0, \infty) and \operatorname{dom}(g) = (-\infty, 1], so sums and products live on the intersection [0, 1]. A quotient additionally removes the zeros of its denominator: g(x) = 0 at x = 1, so f/g loses 1; f(x) = 0 at x = 0, so g/f loses 0.

Adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing — pointwise

All four slides use f(x) = x and g(x) = x^2 - 1, with f(2) = 2, g(2) = 3:

OperationFormulaAt x = 2Remark on the slide
Sum: add the heights(f + g)(x) = x^2 + x - 1(f + g)(2) = 2 + 3 = 5The sum is obtained by combining the two vertical values at the same input.
Difference: subtract the heights(f - g)(x) = -x^2 + x + 1(f - g)(2) = 2 - 3 = -1The difference may be negative even when both original values are positive.
Product: multiply the heights(fg)(x) = x^3 - x(fg)(2) = 2 \cdot 3 = 6The product is zero wherever either factor is zero.
Quotient: watch the denominator\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \dfrac{x}{x^2 - 1}\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(2) = \dfrac{2}{3}Domain: \mathbb{R} \setminus \{-1, 1\}. The quotient is undefined when g(x) = 0.
Common mistake — simplifying away a domain restriction

\dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1} simplifies to x + 1, but the two are different functions: the quotient is undefined at x = 1, the line isn't. Determine the domain from the formula before cancelling, and keep the restriction: \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1} = x + 1 for x \neq 1.

Graph transformations

Shifts

For c, d > 0: f(x) + d shifts the graph up by d; f(x - c) shifts it right by c.

Vertical translation: x^2, x^2 + 1.3, x^2 - 1.2. Horizontal translation: (x + 1.35)^2, x^2, (x - 1.35)^2.

Outside f: change the height. Inside f: move in the opposite direction.

Why does f(x - c) move the graph to the right?

The new function g(x) = f(x - c) takes at x the value that f had at x - c. So whatever f did at the point a now happens at a + c: g(a + c) = f(a). The vertex of x^2 at 0 sits at c for (x - c)^2. The minus sign inside is what "undoes" the shift, hence the opposite direction.

Combine two shifts

Start with f(x) = \lvert x\rvert. To obtain g(x) = \lvert x - 2\rvert - 1, move the graph two units right, then one unit down.

  • Original: f(x) = \lvert x\rvert
  • Step 1: right 2: \lvert x - 2\rvert
  • Step 2: down 1: g(x) = \lvert x - 2\rvert - 1

Watch the vertex: (0, 0) \to (2, 0) \to (2, -1).

Stretching and compression

For c > 1: c\,f(x) stretches vertically, f(cx) compresses horizontally.

Vertical scaling: 2\sqrt{x}, \sqrt{x}, \frac12\sqrt{x}. Horizontal scaling: \sqrt{2x}, \sqrt{x}, \sqrt{x/2}.

Same height y = 1: x = 1 moves to x = \frac12 for f(2x) and to x = 2 for f(x/2).

Reflections

Changing the output sign reflects in the x-axis; changing the input sign reflects in the y-axis.

  • Start with f(x) = \sqrt{x}
  • Reflect across x-axis: -f(x) = -\sqrt{x}
  • Reflect across y-axis: f(-x) = \sqrt{-x}

The coloured points show (4, 2) \mapsto (4, -2) or (4, 2) \mapsto (-4, 2).

Worked example — building g(x) = -2\sqrt{x + 3} + 1 from \sqrt{x}

Inside changes act on x (opposite direction), outside changes on the height; do the inside first, then outside from the innermost operation outwards.

  1. Inside, x + 3: shift left 3 → \sqrt{x + 3}, start point (0, 0) \to (-3, 0).
  2. Outside, \cdot 2: stretch vertically by 2 → 2\sqrt{x + 3}, the point (1, 1) of the original graph is now at (-2, 2).
  3. Outside, minus sign: reflect in the x-axis → -2\sqrt{x + 3}, (-2, 2) \to (-2, -2).
  4. Outside, +1: up 1 → start point (-3, 1), and (-2, -1). Check: g(-3) = -2 \cdot 0 + 1 = 1 ✓, g(-2) = -2 \cdot 1 + 1 = -1 ✓. Domain [-3, \infty), range (-\infty, 1].

Sine waves: amplitude, period and shifts

s(x) = A \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}(x - C)\right) + D, \qquad T > 0, \quad A \neq 0.
Symbols
  • s(x) — the value of the sine wave at x
  • A — its absolute value \lvert A\rvert is the amplitude (half the distance from lowest to highest value); A < 0 additionally reflects the wave
  • T — the period: the wave repeats after every T units of x (T > 0)
  • C — the horizontal shift (phase shift): the wave is moved right by C
  • D — the vertical shift: the midline is the line y = D

Read the parameters: \lvert A\rvert amplitude; T period; C horizontal shift; D vertical shift. The dashed line y = D is the midline. The highest and lowest values are D \pm \lvert A\rvert.

What changes the graph? First compare the amplitude and the period.

  • Changing amplitude \lvert A\rvert: \sin x, 2\sin x, \frac12 \sin x. — Stretch in height: change A.
  • Changing period T: \sin x, \sin(2x), \sin(x/2). — Stretch in width: change T.

Horizontal and vertical shifts. The phase shift C moves the curve horizontally; D moves the midline vertically. Neither changes the amplitude or period.

  • Horizontal shift right \pi/2: \sin x, \sin(x - \pi/2).
  • Vertical shift up 1: \sin x, \sin x + 1.

Inside the sine: horizontal move. Outside the sine: vertical move.

Why is the period T when the formula says \frac{2\pi}{T}?

\sin repeats when its argument grows by 2\pi. The argument \frac{2\pi}{T}(x - C) grows by 2\pi exactly when x grows by T. So writing the factor as \frac{2\pi}{T} makes the period readable directly. If a formula is given as \sin(bx) instead, the period is T = \frac{2\pi}{b}: \sin(2x) has period \pi (faster), \sin(x/2) has period 4\pi (slower).

Worked example — reading s(x) = 3\sin\!\left(2\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right) - 1
  1. Amplitude: \lvert A\rvert = 3.
  2. Period: match \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2 → T = \pi.
  3. Shifts: C = \frac{\pi}{4} (right), D = -1 (midline y = -1).
  4. Range: D \pm \lvert A\rvert → [-4, 2].
  5. Check one point: at x = \frac{\pi}{4} the argument is 0, so s = 3 \cdot 0 - 1 = -1, on the midline and going up ✓.
Connection

This is the AC voltage from the start of the lecture: u(t) = 10\sin(2\pi t) has A = 10 (amplitude 10 V) and \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi, so period T = 1 (one oscillation per second), with no shifts.

Composition: a function inside a function

(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x)).
Symbols
  • f \circ g — read "f composed with g" (or "f after g"): the new function that applies g first, then f
  • g(x) — the intermediate value: the output of g, which becomes the input of f
  • f(g(x)) — the final output

Diagram: x \to g \to g(x) \to f \to f(g(x)). Domain: \{x \in \operatorname{dom}(g) : g(x) \in \operatorname{dom}(f)\}.

Read f \circ g as "f composed with g"; first apply g.

Composition is not commutative

Let f(x) = \sqrt{x} and g(x) = x + 1.

FormulaDomain
f \circ g(f \circ g)(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}[-1, \infty)
g \circ f(g \circ f)(x) = \sqrt{x} + 1[0, \infty)

f \circ g \neq g \circ f in general.

Worked example — domain of a composition

f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}, g(x) = x^2 - 4.

  1. f \circ g, formula: f(g(x)) = \dfrac{1}{x^2 - 4}.
  2. Its domain — two conditions: x \in \operatorname{dom}(g) = \mathbb{R} ✓, and g(x) \in \operatorname{dom}(f), i.e. x^2 - 4 \neq 0 → x \neq \pm 2. Domain \mathbb{R} \setminus \{-2, 2\}.
  3. g \circ f, formula: g(f(x)) = \dfrac{1}{x^2} - 4.
  4. Its domain: x \in \operatorname{dom}(f) = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}, and f(x) \in \operatorname{dom}(g) = \mathbb{R} ✓. Domain \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}. Same two functions, two different compositions with two different domains.
Common mistake — reading f \circ g left to right

f \circ g is written with f first but evaluated with g first, because f(g(x)) is read from the inside out. A safe habit: always rewrite (f \circ g)(x) as f(g(x)) before calculating.

Inverse functions: undo the rule

If f : X \to Y is a bijection, then its inverse f^{-1} : Y \to X satisfies

f^{-1}(f(x)) = x, \quad x \in X, \qquad f(f^{-1}(y)) = y, \quad y \in Y.
Symbols
  • f : X \to Y — a bijection from the set X onto the set Y
  • f^{-1} : Y \to X — its inverse function, going back from Y to X
  • x — any element of X; y — any element of Y

f^{-1} means inverse function. It does not mean 1/f.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 3, f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x - 3}{2}.

Why does only a bijection have an inverse?

f^{-1}(y) must be exactly one x for each y \in Y, i.e. f^{-1} must itself be a function on Y. If f were not injective, some y would come from two x's, and f^{-1}(y) would have two candidates. If f were not surjective, some y would come from no x, and f^{-1}(y) would have no value. Bijective is exactly "every y comes from exactly one x".

An inverse may require a restricted domain

f : [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty), f(x) = x^2, f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x}. f^{-1}(f(x)) = x for x \ge 0. Without restricting the domain, x^2 is not injective.

Intuition — the graph of f^{-1} is the mirror image in y = x

If (a, b) is on the graph of f (f(a) = b), then f^{-1}(b) = a, so (b, a) is on the graph of f^{-1}. Swapping the coordinates of every point is the reflection in the line y = x, visible in the figure: the orange \sqrt{x} is the blue parabola-half flipped over the dashed line.

Find an inverse

Find the inverse of f(x) = 3x - 5.

  1. Write y = 3x - 5.
  2. Solve for x: x = \dfrac{y + 5}{3}.
  3. Swap variable names: f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x + 5}{3}.
  4. Check f^{-1}(f(x)) = x.

General fact: (g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} when both are invertible.

Worked example — inverse of f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3} on \mathbb{R} \setminus \{3\}
  1. Write y = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}.
  2. Clear the denominator: y(x - 3) = 2x + 1 \Rightarrow yx - 2x = 3y + 1.
  3. Collect x and solve: x(y - 2) = 3y + 1 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{3y + 1}{y - 2}, possible for every y \neq 2. So the range is \mathbb{R} \setminus \{2\}, and f : \mathbb{R} \setminus \{3\} \to \mathbb{R} \setminus \{2\} is a bijection.
  4. Swap names: f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x + 1}{x - 2}, x \neq 2.
  5. Check: f^{-1}(f(0)) = f^{-1}\!\left(-\tfrac13\right) = \dfrac{-1 + 1}{-\tfrac13 - 2} = 0 ✓.
Why is (g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} and not g^{-1} \circ f^{-1}?

g \circ f applies f first, then g. To undo it, you must undo the last step first: first g^{-1}, then f^{-1}, which is f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} (again read inside out). Like getting dressed: socks then shoes; undressing: shoes then socks. Check: (f^{-1} \circ g^{-1})(g(f(x))) = f^{-1}(g^{-1}(g(f(x)))) = f^{-1}(f(x)) = x.

Common mistake — f^{-1} is not 1/f

For f(x) = 3x - 5, f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x+5}{3}, while \frac{1}{f(x)} = \frac{1}{3x - 5}: completely different functions. The superscript -1 on a function means "inverse"; on a number it means "reciprocal". The same trap returns with \sin^{-1} x (= \arcsin x, not \frac{1}{\sin x}), even though \sin^2 x does mean (\sin x)^2.

Inverse trigonometric functions

domain → range
\arcsin[-1, 1] \to [-\pi/2, \pi/2]\sin(\arcsin x) = x for x \in [-1, 1]
\arccos[-1, 1] \to [0, \pi]\arcsin(\sin x) = x only if x \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]
\arctan\mathbb{R} \to (-\pi/2, \pi/2)

Restriction to one branch makes the inverse single-valued.

Inverse sine: choosing a branch. The sine function becomes invertible when restricted to [-\pi/2, \pi/2]. Its inverse is \arcsin x (also written \sin^{-1} x). \sin : [-\pi/2, \pi/2] \to [-1, 1]; \arcsin : [-1, 1] \to [-\pi/2, \pi/2]. Example: \arcsin(1/2) = \pi/6. Here \sin^{-1} does not mean the reciprocal 1/\sin.

Inverse cosine: choosing a branch. The cosine function becomes invertible when restricted to [0, \pi]. Its inverse is \arccos x (also written \cos^{-1} x). \cos : [0, \pi] \to [-1, 1]; \arccos : [-1, 1] \to [0, \pi]. Example: \arccos(0) = \pi/2. Notice: \arccos is decreasing.

Inverse tangent: an infinite domain. The tangent function is invertible on (-\pi/2, \pi/2). Its inverse \arctan x is defined for every real number. \tan : (-\pi/2, \pi/2) \to \mathbb{R}; \arctan : \mathbb{R} \to (-\pi/2, \pi/2). The inverse-tangent graph approaches \pm\pi/2 but never reaches these values.

Why these branches, and why is \arccos decreasing?

Each branch is an interval on which the function is strictly monotone (hence injective) and still takes every value once: sine increases from -1 to 1 on [-\pi/2, \pi/2], tangent increases from -\infty to \infty on (-\pi/2, \pi/2), cosine decreases from 1 to -1 on [0, \pi]. Sine can't use [0, \pi] (it goes up and down there), cosine can't use [-\pi/2, \pi/2] (same problem). The inverse of a decreasing function is decreasing, so \arccos goes down from \pi at -1 to 0 at 1.

Worked example — \arcsin(\sin x) outside the branch

\arcsin\!\left(\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}\right):

  1. Inner value: \sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac12.
  2. Outer value — must lie in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]: the angle there with sine \frac12 is \frac{\pi}{6}.
  3. Result: \frac{\pi}{6}, not \frac{5\pi}{6}, because \frac{5\pi}{6} \notin [-\pi/2, \pi/2]. That is the slide's warning "\arcsin(\sin x) = x only if x \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]".

Elementary and transcendental functions

Algebraic examples: \sqrt{1 + x^2}, \dfrac{x + 1}{x^2 + 1}. Transcendental examples: e^x, \sin x, \ln x.

An elementary function can be built using finitely many arithmetic operations and compositions from algebraic, exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions.

"Elementary" describes a class of functions, not their difficulty.

Intuition — algebraic vs. transcendental

Algebraic = built from x with +, -, \cdot, \div and roots only (the earlier families up to "algebraic functions"). A transcendental function is one that is not algebraic, like e^x, \sin x, \ln x. "Elementary" is the bigger box that contains both kinds and everything you can build from them by combining and composing.

An elementary function

Elementary does not mean algebraic. For example, f(x) = e^{-x/3}\cos(4x) is elementary but non-algebraic.

Graph: f(x) oscillating between the dashed curves e^{-x/3} and -e^{-x/3}, for 0 \le x \le 12.

An oscillation whose amplitude decreases – a simple model of damping.

A non-elementary function: the error function

A non-elementary function cannot be obtained from a finite combination of standard elementary functions using the usual operations and composition. One example is the error function.

\operatorname{erf}(x) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^x e^{-t^2}\, dt.
Symbols
  • \operatorname{erf}(x) — the error function at x (dimensionless)
  • t — the integration variable, running from 0 to x
  • e^{-t^2} — the bell-shaped Gaussian curve being integrated
  • \int_0^x \dots\, dt — the (signed) area under that curve between 0 and x; integrals come later in the course
  • \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} — a constant chosen so that the values approach \pm 1

Basic properties: \operatorname{erf}(0) = 0; \operatorname{erf}(-x) = -\operatorname{erf}(x); -1 < \operatorname{erf}(x) < 1.

Used in probability and measurement theory. The integral is a preview; no calculation is needed here.

Optional reference: inequalities

Arithmetic–geometric mean (a_j \ge 0):

\frac{a_1 + \dots + a_n}{n} \ge \sqrt[n]{a_1 \cdots a_n}.
Symbols
  • a_1, \dots, a_n — n non-negative real numbers
  • left side — their arithmetic mean (the usual average); right side — their geometric mean

Bernoulli (t \ge -1, n \in \mathbb{N}): (1 + t)^n \ge 1 + nt.

Cauchy–Schwarz (a_j, b_j \in \mathbb{R}):

\left(\sum_{j=1}^n a_j b_j\right)^2 \le \left(\sum_{j=1}^n a_j^2\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j^2\right).
Symbols
  • a_j, b_j — two lists of n real numbers (j = 1, \dots, n)
  • \sum_{j=1}^n — sum over j from 1 to n

Further inequalities. Let p, q > 1 with 1/p + 1/q = 1.

  • Young (a, b \ge 0): ab \le \dfrac{a^p}{p} + \dfrac{b^q}{q}.
  • Hölder: \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^n \lvert a_j b_j\rvert \le \Bigl(\sum \lvert a_j\rvert^p\Bigr)^{1/p} \Bigl(\sum \lvert b_j\rvert^q\Bigr)^{1/q}.
  • Minkowski: \displaystyle\Bigl(\sum \lvert a_j + b_j\rvert^p\Bigr)^{1/p} \le \Bigl(\sum \lvert a_j\rvert^p\Bigr)^{1/p} + \Bigl(\sum \lvert b_j\rvert^p\Bigr)^{1/p}.
Why is AM–GM true for two numbers?

For a, b \ge 0: 0 \le (\sqrt a - \sqrt b)^2 = a - 2\sqrt{ab} + b, so \frac{a + b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}, with equality exactly when a = b. Example: a = 4, b = 9: mean 6.5 \ge 6 = \sqrt{36}. Bernoulli is just as easy to try out: (1.01)^{10} \approx 1.1046 \ge 1.1 = 1 + 10 \cdot 0.01.
